product.minus: The stated 30-40 minute window routinely stretches to an hour and a half or two: the app shows an optimistic ETA, then silently pushes it back after you've ordered. For food at home that means a cold plate by the time it lands.

product.title: Support answers only with AI bots that deny refunds
product.minus: Reaching a human is nearly impossible: it's all AI that copy-pastes the same replies and loops the conversation. Even after getting a person, users are told a refund «isn't eligible», and each email is handled by a different agent from scratch.

product.title: Orders get accepted, then cancelled — often after the food is already made
product.minus: Confirmed orders get cancelled for lack of drivers, sometimes 15 minutes before delivery, with the blame shifted to the restaurant. Yet you can't cancel yourself: once accepted the button locks, leaving you on hold for an hour.

product.title: After «too many» complaints they block your ability to request refunds
product.minus: If a user reports problems «too often», the account gets flagged and permanently loses the right to a refund — even when the restaurant or driver is at fault. The customer is punished for others' mistakes and forced to pay for food never received.

product.title: Instead of a real refund they push a $5 credit that expires in 30 days
product.minus: When an order is botched or undelivered, the company offers a $5 credit instead of cash — one that expires in 30 days and forces you back into the app. For a late $50 order, the token feels like mockery, not compensation.

product.title: Drivers steal food and confirm delivery with fake photos
product.minus: A frequent complaint: the driver keeps the food and «confirms» delivery with a photo of a random sign or a blacked-out frame. Grubhub then refuses a refund, leaving the customer with neither food nor money.

product.title: The «contactless» PIN must be handed over in person — and it's used to steal food
product.minus: In the name of security the app demands you give the driver a PIN in person, turning contactless delivery into contact delivery. Worse: drivers beg for the PIN by text to «close» the order and drive off with the food, while support blames the customer.

product.title: The final price jumps at checkout: markups and a fan of hidden fees
product.minus: In-app prices run higher than the restaurant's own, then service fee, delivery and tip pile on — the total can jump $20 after you hit checkout. Even with the paid Plus membership the fees stay predatory.

product.title: Promo codes and «discounts» don't apply at checkout
product.minus: Promised new-user discounts and 30-35% coupons routinely «expire» or simply fail to apply in either the app or the website. It works as bait to make you download the app, but the actual savings never materialize.

product.title: The app breaks at payment: errors with no explanation and broken buttons
product.minus: At checkout vague errors like «This field is required» and «Something went wrong» appear without saying what to fix; Google Pay fails, +/- buttons don't work, and you can't add a card. Some users only get through by switching to the website.

product.title: Orders arrive incomplete or mixed up, and no one checks them
product.minus: Drinks go missing, the wrong order shows up, items get swapped — and refunds cover only the missing part, even when the rest is inedible without it. No one on Grubhub's side checks the order before handoff.

product.title: Linking Amazon Prime doesn't deliver the promised free delivery or Grubhub+
product.minus: The Prime link is sold as free delivery, but in practice the Amazon sign-in glitches, Grubhub+ never activates, and unlinking is a dark-pattern nightmare. The same fees you'd pay without Prime stay in place.

product.title: For happy users, the Prime pairing saves it: free delivery and low fees
product.plus: Satisfied users uniformly praise the Amazon Prime pairing: delivery drops to $0 even where the fee was $6.99, and the yearly membership genuinely saves money. For this group Grubhub comes out cheaper than DoorDash.

product.title: When it works — fast, easy, and with friendly drivers
product.plus: For the loyal slice of the audience — many homebound or disabled — the experience is the opposite: hot food, polite drivers, on-time or early delivery. For them the app is simple, dependable, and a years-long lifeline.

product.title: Some users praise support and fewer mistakes versus DoorDash
product.plus: A minority reports the opposite support experience: issues resolved fast and kindly, refunds issued without a fight when something goes wrong. Head-to-head against DoorDash it favors Grubhub — fewer mistakes, drinks arriving without spills.

product.title: The promised delivery window is fiction: it gets pushed hours later, even with paid priority
product.minus: The single most common complaint: an order promised by 2pm slides to 4pm, then to the next day, on repeat. Paid priority and rush don't help — people wait 5-7 hours, miss dinner and end up cancelling themselves.

product.title: The real price is a markup on every item plus layers of fees on top of "free delivery"
product.minus: People compare the bill to the in-store price tag and find a 10-20% markup per item, then service fees, delivery fees and store markup on top. Even shoppers admit the customer pays at least a dollar more per product. The "free delivery" turns out to be paid for.

product.title: Instacart+ membership gets signed up without consent and then they refuse to cancel it
product.minus: Again and again: a user explicitly declines membership, then wakes up to a welcome email and a $49 yearly charge. The signup button sits right next to checkout, and the annual plan drains the account. Cancelling is "too late" and no refund follows.

product.title: Support is a bot that loops, and live agents drop the chat and punish you with delays
product.minus: Dry AI replies with no apology, a chatbot going in circles, agents ending the chat with no solution. Worse: people say complaining gets their order deliberately pushed back hours. "Help" boils down to a $5 credit and "we understand your concern."

product.title: The app freezes on the login screen: buttons won't press, the screen is "frozen"
product.minus: A whole layer of reviews: people simply can't get in — taps don't register, the sign in / log in buttons are dead, the screen hangs with an ad banner on top. Reinstalling doesn't help; they fall back to the web version or just delete the app.

product.title: The shopper "forgets" items, flags them out of stock, or swaps in a bad replacement
product.minus: A constant pain: half the list arrives, the rest is "out of stock" — though the store has it. Heavy or fussy items get refunded too readily instead of found. Replacements are poorly chosen and unapproved. The result is the very thing they ordered to avoid: going to the store yourself.

product.title: Perishables arrive warm and spoiled: melted ice cream, slimy onions, rotten meat
product.minus: No temperature control: ice cream and milk ride in a hot trunk at 90°+, melting over two hours of detours. Near-expired produce, rotten meat and slimy onions show up — and refunds for spoiled goods are often denied.

product.title: Order marked "delivered" to the wrong door or street — and they won't retrieve it
product.minus: Drivers ignore instructions and apartment numbers, dumping bags at the wrong door or on a street the customer doesn't live on. The status says "delivered" but nothing arrived, and no one offers to go fetch it — especially brutal for people post-surgery who can't go out.

product.title: Money disappears unexpectedly: extra holds, double tips, charges attempted without consent
product.minus: People catch unauthorized charge attempts, double tip charges, and holds triple the price of an added item. Customers can strip tips retroactively, leaving shoppers robbed. Fraudulent card charges get deflected onto the third-party Uber backend.

product.title: For those who can't get out, it's a lifeline — an attentive shopper who hands it straight to you
product.plus: The warmest layer of reviews: the elderly, disabled, post-surgery and car-less call it a "godsend." Shoppers carry groceries to the door and into your hands, bring them inside, send photos of produce, pick ripe fruit — this is the value that keeps people loyal.

product.title: When it works, it's effortless: a wide choice of stores and fast delivery
product.plus: For a chunk of users it's seamless: an easy app, time to browse and zoom in to read labels, lots of stores to pick from. Delivery is fast and accurate, sometimes early, couriers are polite. For them, Instacart is something they can't imagine living without.

product.title: Restaurant delivery is bolted on via Uber Eats and works poorly: prices shift, no tipping
product.minus: Restaurant delivery, sub-contracted through Uber Eats, is the weak spot: receipts lag, you can't tip the driver after delivery, times are inaccurate, and missing orders get no refund. Seasoned users advise skipping the feature entirely.

product.title: Support was replaced by an AI bot that loops endlessly and helps with nothing
product.minus: When something goes wrong, users hit a chatbot that won't let them type the actual problem, gives inconsistent answers, and routes the «live agent» to yet another AI. Reaching a real human or phone line is nearly impossible.

product.title: They deny refunds even when the order never arrived or items are missing
product.minus: The single most common pain: items missing, order never delivered, or wrong order — and support declares it «not eligible for a refund». «GPS says they stopped at the right spot» becomes the universal excuse to refuse, even against photo proof.

product.title: Fees and service charges routinely exceed the cost of the food itself
product.minus: A $7 sub picks up $9 in fees; a $10 meal becomes $20+. Charges stack up (service fee, menu markup, delivery), and users keep concluding that ordering directly from the restaurant is cheaper.

product.title: Food arrives cold because drivers stack multiple orders along the way
product.minus: Once Uber let drivers accept multiple orders at once, hot food consistently arrives cold and frozen goods melt. The «priority» upcharge feels like ransom for what the subscription used to include.

product.title: Promos and discounts vanish at checkout, leaving you paying full price
product.minus: A discount applies in the cart, then silently drops at payment and the full amount is charged. Support later claims the user «wasn't eligible» for the very promo the app advertised to them.

product.title: You can't cancel without a penalty, even seconds after placing the order
product.minus: There's a «cancel» button, but using it charges the full price plus a cancellation fee with no refund. Support replies that you «should have contacted them before cancelling» — making the button a trap.

product.title: Tips can only be raised after delivery, never lowered
product.minus: You're pushed to tip before delivery and then blocked from reducing it, even when food is dumped at the wrong door in the rain. The tip field is also calculated on the total including fees and taxes, inflating an honest 20% by half again.

product.title: The algorithm assigns a far-away restaurant instead of the one nearby
product.minus: You pick a chain with a branch 2 miles away, and the order gets routed to one 30 miles out, turning a 15-minute delivery into an hour and a half. The driver-facing maps are outdated and routes constantly go wrong.

product.title: Uber One signup is dropped right next to the checkout button
product.minus: The Uber One signup button sits so close to the order button that users hit it by accident, and even after cancelling they keep getting charged for months. The relentless join-now screen reads as a dark pattern.

product.title: Drivers steal or dump the food, and the company sides with them
product.minus: A driver snaps a «delivered» photo and drives off with the food, leaves it at someone else's door, or eats it outright — and the user still pays. Support believes the driver, leaving the customer out of pocket and hungry.

product.title: They charge your card for orders that never reach the restaurant
product.minus: The card is charged but the order never reaches the courier, hangs for hours, then simply disappears from the queue along with the money. Double charges and phantom payments happen with no way to dispute them.

product.title: First-time promo codes actually work and are genuinely generous
product.plus: Many users single out the welcome offers: $20–25 off the first order, up to 30% off — and unlike later promos, the starter codes actually apply at checkout.

product.title: For loyal users it's convenient, fast, and a lifesaver without a car
product.plus: A core of long-time users is genuinely happy: ordering is simple, deliveries arrive on time, the restaurant selection is wide, and it's indispensable when you can't or won't drive for food yourself.

product.title: No status updates — you never know where the food is or when it'll arrive
product.minus: The app won't show where the order is in the process or whether it's ready, yet floods you with spam notifications carrying no real info. The promised delivery time keeps sliding later, then «still on time» becomes the excuse to deny a refund.

product.title: Driver quality collapsed after the Uber merger
product.minus: Long-time users note that since the Uber acquisition drivers stopped reading instructions, don't speak English, won't come to the marked spot, and juggle several apps at once. The app that was «king» in the pandemic has visibly degraded.

product.title: Payment friction: cards rejected, Uber Cash forced on you
product.minus: The app rejects working cards, claims «insufficient funds» on a full balance, and auto-selects Uber Cash that then can't be used — turning checkout into a 20-minute fight. Sometimes a new card can't be added at all due to a constant error.

product.title: Forced ID verification and robot delivery you can't opt out of
product.minus: Ordering alcohol or even placing a delivery demands an ID scan the camera won't focus on — and users fear their photo ID being leaked. Robot delivery is opt-out by default, and you can only decline it 8 days at a time.

product.title: Broken browsing: category navigation gone, restaurants «unavailable»
product.minus: An update killed browsing by cuisine — without the exact restaurant name you get «We didn't find a match». For some users every restaurant opens as «unavailable», making the app useless even after reinstalling.

product.title: Support is a wall: one «we can't do anything» script for every problem
product.minus: The single most common complaint: when an order goes wrong, support replies with copy-paste, won't escalate, and refuses refunds. You first have to fight through an AI bot, only to reach a human repeating the same script.

product.title: Missing items, no refund: half the order never arrives and the money stays gone
product.minus: Orders routinely arrive incomplete, and the refund for what's missing is either denied or a token few pounds. To get the missing item you have to re-order and pay delivery all over again.

product.title: Cold food from stacking: drivers carry other orders while yours sits going cold
product.minus: By making drivers pick up two orders at once, your food sits in the box while someone else's is cooked and arrives stone cold, soggy and sweaty. It's a platform design choice, not one driver's fault.

product.title: Bait offers: the new-user discount is stripped off at the final payment step
product.minus: Ads promise «50% / AED 50 off for new users», but at checkout the system demands you remove the voucher to pay, or silently strips it. Often the order goes through at full price anyway, with no refund.

product.title: Plus/Gold is nearly impossible to cancel — you have to delete the account
product.minus: Cancelling is buried behind forms and loops; the switch-plans button doesn't work. Some users were subscribed without consent, and the only way out is to delete the whole account.

product.title: Prices inflated over the restaurant, then a forest of fees on top of everything
product.minus: The same items cost more in the app than in-restaurant or at pickup, and on top come a service fee, a small-order fee, a picking fee. Even with a discount it's pricier than going direct.

product.title: Delivery estimates are fiction: «20 minutes» easily becomes an hour or more
product.minus: The quoted delivery time is systematically optimistic and keeps extending while the app flips between «finding the driver» and «driver heading to restaurant». Without paid express, the wait often doubles.

product.title: Payment just fails: cards «invalid», cash not accepted, order falls through
product.minus: Many users simply can't pay — the app rejects several cards in a row and won't take cash. Money gets deducted, the order fails, and the refund never lands back in the account.

product.title: Orders accepted then cancelled: restaurant long closed, but money already taken
product.minus: The app accepts the order and takes payment, then cancels 20-45 minutes later — often from a restaurant that has stopped working with Deliveroo entirely. You can't cancel it yourself.

product.title: The app crashes, won't load, and drains the battery
product.minus: Freezes, crashes, a green start-up screen and login errors like HT409 — clearing cache and reinstalling don't help. One user reports a 20-minute order eats half the battery.

product.title: Ads inside a paid app: banners even on the order-tracking screen
product.minus: People pay for Plus and service fees yet still get ads — including banners on the order-tracking screen and pushy ad notifications you can't disable without killing delivery updates too.

product.title: Coverage is big-city only: outside London the app is simply useless
product.minus: In smaller towns there are zero available restaurants or the address is out of zone, and has been for years. Users wait years for their area to launch and eventually give up.

product.title: When it works, it's fast, convenient, with friendly drivers
product.plus: Happy users praise a smooth, convenient app, fast reliable delivery and polite drivers. For many it's a lifeline — especially when they can't get to the shops themselves.

product.title: The 2-digit confirmation code and Prime bundle are where Deliveroo beats rivals
product.plus: Loyal users note Deliveroo's support beats Uber Eats and Just Eat, a handy 2-digit code instead of a 4-digit one, in-app tipping, and an Amazon Prime link for free delivery.

product.title: Refunds are clawed back like a favour — even with proof
product.minus: The single most common and defining pain: for undelivered, wrong or spoiled orders Just Eat routinely refuses refunds, hides behind «previous claims», and closes the case without explanation — even when photos and proof are attached.

product.title: «Delivered» but nothing arrives: drivers mark it done and vanish
product.minus: A very frequent scenario: the courier marks the order delivered though nothing arrived, and the system automatically treats the dispute as closed — users flatly call it drivers stealing the food.

product.title: No human to reach — just a looping AI bot
product.minus: Support is effectively fully automated: an AI chat gives canned replies, refuses to connect a human, closes the chat or traps you in an endless loop, and the phone line hands you to a robot.

product.title: Restaurant reviews removed — now you order blind
product.minus: Hiding written customer reviews is seen as deliberate deception: users believe weak venues are artificially shown as five-star, and there's no way to tell where you're ordering from.

product.title: Discounts and promos are bait — at checkout it's «not available»
product.minus: Promised first-order discounts and offers like buy-one-get-one routinely fail to apply: the total doesn't drop at checkout, and with markups the «discounted» price ends up higher than in-store.

product.title: Fee on fee on fee: delivery, service, tips — cheaper to collect yourself
product.minus: Multiple per-order fees, item markups and a tip prompt before delivery inflate the total by around 50%, and many advise calling the restaurant directly or collecting yourself.

product.title: You can't cancel, they cancel for you — and leave you with cold food
product.minus: There's no in-app cancel button, yet the service itself cancels after an hour or more of waiting «due to driver shortage», by which point restaurants have closed and the food has gone cold.

product.title: A barrage of notifications that won't stop even when you disable them
product.minus: Marketing pushes arrive several times a day, including early morning, and keep coming even after every notification is switched off — users threaten to report it to the regulator.

product.title: Food turns up cold, spilled and incomplete
product.minus: Recurring complaints about cold soggy food, drinks spilled half-empty and items missing at handover — followed, again, by refused compensation.

product.title: When it works — easy ordering, hot food and polite drivers
product.plus: A real share of happy users: the app is easy to use, the choice of restaurants is wide, food arrives hot and fast, and drivers are polite — for loyal users it's a convenient, familiar way to order dinner.

product.title: Fast refunds — but only for a happy minority
product.plus: Some long-term users report the opposite experience: when an order is wrong or an item is out of stock, the money comes back within a day — and that's exactly why they rate Just Eat above rivals.

product.title: Loses the map and address, screens hang, login fails
product.minus: Technical faults: the map shows the wrong delivery address, the payment screen loads forever, delivery notes get swapped, and sign-in sometimes dies on «Something went wrong».

product.title: Support is a bot that loops and never lets you reach a human
product.minus: The defining pain: any order problem dead-ends in an AI chat that repeats scripted replies, refuses to admit fault, and blocks access to a real agent. Users describe it as a deliberate tactic to exhaust them until they give up.

product.title: Money taken, order cancelled — and no refund
product.minus: A very frequent complaint: for missing, spoiled, or undelivered orders the refund either never comes or lands as a tiny voucher in the Zomato Wallet that expires in a day — effectively forcing you to order again.

product.title: One rider carries three orders — so everything arrives late
product.minus: A structural cause of lateness: the app stacks several orders on a single rider, so a 40-minute delivery becomes 75 minutes or an hour and a half, with the food detouring to other people's addresses on the way.

product.title: The on-screen ETA is fiction — reality is double
product.minus: The time estimate openly lies: 15 minutes at checkout becomes 20, then 45, and the actual arrival lands at double the promise. Users flatly advise ignoring the timer and ordering from a local vendor instead.

product.title: Cancellation exists on screen but is effectively impossible or fully charged
product.minus: Even cancelling two minutes after placing the order eats the entire amount, and often the cancel button simply doesn't work. Users call it a trap: the order is still delivered hours late and the money never comes back.

product.title: Orders arrive incomplete or with swapped dishes
product.minus: A recurring issue: two items become one, veg biryani turns into egg, bhakari turns into chapati, and quantities are wrong. The compensation is a token ₹70 voucher that solves nothing.

product.title: Riders mark orders 'delivered' without ever handing over the food
product.minus: A distinct flavor of cheating: the rider marks the order delivered with no food in hand, claims to have called and never shows, or drives past the address and parks a kilometre away. Calling support is useless — a bot answers.

product.title: Stacked fees on top of price: platform, packaging, markup — even with Gold
product.minus: What grates isn't one price but the layers of fees: platform and packaging charges hit even Gold members, and the item itself costs up to three times the in-store price. Some users openly call for a boycott.

product.title: Zomato food is worse than the same restaurant in person
product.minus: Quality suffers specifically through delivery: the same restaurants serve fresh food in-house, but via the app it arrives stale, off-smelling, spilled, and sometimes spoiled — a mouldy cake, expired laddus, uncooked bread.

product.title: When it works — fast, tasty, and around the clock
product.plus: Amid the complaints there are genuine thank-yous: food arrives fast and tasty, the app saves you at night (an order at 4:30 a.m. still shows up), it's handy for emergencies, and the final bill matches the listed price with no checkout surprises.

product.title: Requests for a tracking widget, review editing, and accessibility
product.minus: Concrete feature gaps users explicitly ask for: no live delivery-tracker widget on the lock screen, no way to edit a review or add photos to an order, and the app is effectively inaccessible for people with disabilities.

product.title: A promised 30 minutes turns into one or two hours
product.minus: The single most common complaint: the ETA says 30 minutes but the food shows up after an hour, ninety minutes, or even two hours — lunch arrives at dinnertime, even when the restaurant is just down the street.

product.title: You can't cancel — yet they charge the full cancellation fee
product.minus: Users cancel within two minutes of ordering, or the app won't let them cancel at all, yet they still get charged 100% of the order as a "cancellation fee" — many call it a deliberate scam by design.

product.title: Support is a looping bot that resolves nothing
product.minus: The chat assistant runs the same script in circles, ignores "Human"/"Escalate"/"Manager", and live reps hang up the call — complaints get closed with no resolution, and the help mode is called a flat-out joke.

product.title: Orders marked "delivered" while the courier is kilometers away
product.minus: The delivery partner marks the order "delivered" while far from the address (visible on Swiggy's own map), then SMS the customer asking for the OTP for food they never got — that's a fraud risk, not a delivery.

product.title: The "on-time" timer is rewritten to hide the delay
product.minus: The app retroactively changes the "expected" time to show the order as "on time" while it's clearly late; the Black on-time guarantee often never even starts, even when the food is already out for delivery.

product.title: Taxes, fees and delivery inflate the bill several times over
product.minus: GST, platform, delivery and "rain" fees easily add ~₹200, item prices run several times the restaurant's own menu, and the amount changes at the payment screen — users leave for Zomato over the cost.

product.title: Wrong items, missing items — and no refund
product.minus: Items go missing or arrive completely wrong — chicken instead of veg, the wrong cut of meat — and even when the courier confirms the shortage, they hand out a token coupon instead of a refund.

product.title: Food arrives cold, spoiled and unsafe
product.minus: Food arrives cold and expired, with insects, rotten produce, melted ice cream, curd in a plastic bag — and complaints get closed with a reply that it was "prepared with standard method."

product.title: No courier assigned, no answer, or a demand for extra cash
product.minus: Couriers go unassigned for ages, the assigned one won't pick up, no replacement is sent when a bike breaks down, and some demand extra cash or refuse to come up to the floor.

product.title: Refunds never arrive or drag on for weeks
product.minus: Refunds either never come or are promised in "14-15 days" / "3 slots" while the bank confirms nothing arrived; for undelivered food or clear defects they refuse a refund and offer a useless coupon.

product.title: No cash on delivery — and no ordering without prepay
product.minus: The lack of cash on delivery erodes trust: with prepay people lose money on undelivered orders, whereas COD would remove the risk — some users dock stars purely for this.

product.title: When it works — fast, convenient, and a kind courier
product.plus: The satisfied minority praises the wide restaurant selection, easy-to-use interface, fast delivery and kind couriers, with special love for Instamart and the convenience of COD where it's offered.

product.title: A forced AI assistant replacing the familiar catalog enraged loyal customers
product.minus: An update threw out the familiar category browsing and pushed a Grok/SpaceX-powered "Go" chatbot with no way to opt out: people who were fans for years are now leaving over unwanted, intrusive AI that slows the app down and adds items to the cart on its own.

product.title: Support is a scripted bot you can't get past to reach a human
product.minus: Any problem is funneled into a chatbot that repeats the same scripted answer, ends the chat and refuses to connect you to a human; you used to reach a live agent in minutes, now it's endless circles.

product.title: They take your money, and you have to fight for weeks to get a refund
product.minus: Cancellations aren't refunded automatically: for a missing, spoiled or undelivered order they offer a tiny credit instead of money, drag refunds out for 48+ hours, and people end up forced to chargeback through their bank or PayPal.

product.title: The promised 15-30 minutes turns into hours of waiting in reality
product.minus: The app promises delivery in 15-30 minutes, but finding a driver takes an hour or two, the order is 90+ minutes late even when the warehouse is minutes away, and sometimes it's just cancelled toward morning.

product.title: The FAM membership is pushed on you and impossible to cancel
product.minus: The interface nudges you into accidentally subscribing to the paid family plan, then charges you for months and even after you've moved out of the delivery zone; there's no way to cancel in the app, and out of region no way at all to stop the charges.

product.title: A forced 20-30% default tip on every single order
product.minus: Tips default to 20-30% on top of delivery and service fees, and you have to manually zero them out every time or you accidentally tip; and if the order is missing or broken, they suggest you just stop tipping instead of taking responsibility.

product.title: Groceries arrive spoiled, crushed or stale
product.minus: Complaints about spoiled meat, moldy bread, crushed berries and out-of-date food; on repeat spoilage they refuse refunds "per policy," turning a mundane annoyance into a food-safety issue.

product.title: Prices 2-3x store level plus a pile of hidden fees
product.minus: After third-party markups and delivery/service fees it comes out 2-3x more than the same groceries in store — you pay a premium for convenience, and many find it excessive.

product.title: Delivery zones vanish suddenly, leaving paid memberships useless
product.minus: A nearby warehouse closes or the delivery zone is pulled with no notice — sometimes after you move a couple of miles or pay for a yearly membership — and your saved points and membership simply evaporate.

product.title: Broken sign-in and endless ID re-scans lock you out of ordering
product.minus: Registration and login constantly fail: it won't accept your phone number, foreign country codes or SNAP pin; and the age-verification ID scan has to be redone every single order, even after dozens of successful deliveries.

product.title: When it works, it's fast, convenient and a lifeline for the housebound
product.plus: The core love is speed and convenience: orders often in 10-30 minutes, late-night and 24/7 hours, which is especially a lifeline for disabled, sick and housebound users who struggle to get out for groceries and snacks.

product.title: One late-night store for everything: alcohol, tobacco, vapes and snacks till 3am
product.plus: The unique niche is delivering alcohol, cigarettes, vapes and THC products alongside groceries and snacks late at night; for midnight munchies, parties and "need it now" moments it's the main reason people stick around.

product.title: Polite, fast drivers are a frequent reason for five stars
product.plus: Many praise couriers by name: polite, precisely following instructions, giving dogs treats and getting the order right and on time — the personal touch from the driver is often the standout positive experience.

product.title: Rude couriers, theft and "delivered" without delivery wreck the experience
product.minus: The flip side — drivers stay silent and rude even with big tips, leave bags outside the gate, mark orders delivered without handing them over, and sometimes outright steal the items, with the service taking no responsibility.

product.title: The method rewires your relationship with money — fans say it changed their lives
product.plus: The most frequent praise isn't about features but outcomes: people climb out of debt, start saving, and stop guessing whether they can afford something. The give-every-dollar-a-job approach lifts the anxiety around spending.

product.title: The forced 2025 Home tab added clicks and pulled the add-transaction button off the budget screen
product.minus: The September redesign opens the app on a new Home tab users call useless instead of the budget, and the add-transaction button was removed from the plan screen, so logging a purchase quickly on the go — the core use case — now takes several extra clicks. There's no way to turn the tab off.

product.title: The most expensive budgeting app: $15/mo, $100+/yr, with no free tier
product.minus: Ironically pricey for an app meant to help you save: $15/month or $100+/year with no free version. Many bail the moment they see the price, calling uninstalling it "the best budget decision." Yearly price hikes wear down even loyal users.

product.title: The price is hidden until the end of onboarding: 20 questions, email signup, then the paywall
product.minus: The app walks you through a pile of questions and an email signup, then only at the end reveals it's a paid subscription with no free tier. Users call this deliberately misleading and distrust an app that opens this way.

product.title: Bank sync keeps breaking — and it's the main feature people pay for
product.minus: Automatic transaction import is the main reason to pay, yet the bank connection drops every few weeks, needs re-authentication sometimes several times a day, and then everything must be entered by hand. EU users lost sync entirely after a provider switch.

product.title: Constant UI redesigns force you to relearn the app monthly — long-time fans are furious
product.minus: Every update reshuffles things, and decade-long users complain they have to relearn where features live almost monthly. Many feel the developers are "fixing what isn't broken" and stop recommending the app.

product.title: Manually assigning every dollar and approving every transaction — a steep learning curve
product.minus: The method requires manually assigning every dollar to categories and approving each transaction, which confuses newcomers and busy people. Many call it unintuitive and overcomplicated for basic tasks, quitting during category setup.

product.title: Ads for its own products and the founder's book — inside a $100+ subscription
product.minus: Inside a $100+/year paid subscription, users get pop-up ads for YNAB's own products and the founder's book preorder. Paying subscribers find this brazen and a betrayal of the user base.

product.title: Cancelling and refunds are made deliberately hard — no in-app cancel, no refunds given
product.minus: You can't cancel in the app — it pushes you to a desktop website whose links reopen in the app. Refunds are refused even when features are broken, with blame pinned on Google. Several users found themselves auto-subscribed for a year after minutes of use.

product.title: App buttons collide with Samsung/Android navigation — split transactions become impossible
product.minus: On Samsung and Android devices the "0", "Done" and back buttons in split mode sit right on top of the phone's system navigation bar, so you can't tap them and can't split a transaction across categories. The app doesn't scale to the usable screen area.

product.title: No bi-weekly cycle — yet many people are paid every two weeks
product.minus: The app plans monthly and doesn't support a bi-weekly (every-two-weeks) pay cycle, even though many people are paid that way. You end up constantly reallocating by hand — the promised automation for a biweekly budget basically isn't there.

product.title: Shared budgeting for couples works — but two-person sync stumbles
product.plus: A beloved feature for couples and families: a shared budget on both phones, both seeing spending in real time and checking in before a purchase. For many it's the reason they could finally budget together.

product.title: Subscription cancellation is sold as magic but barely works
product.minus: The headline promise from the ads — "we'll find and cancel for you" — fails for many: the app either cancels one of several, or just hands you a list telling you to call/email each company yourself, or lies that it canceled.

product.title: Bank linking loops endlessly: you approve, then it asks you to link again
product.minus: One of the most common failure modes: you go through the whole bank login, the bank approves access, you return to the app — and it resets and demands you link the account again. People repeat this 3, 8, 50 times and give up.

product.title: The free tier is hollow — you pay a subscription to track subscriptions
product.minus: Users hate the paradox itself: an app that helps cancel subscriptions only works behind its own paid subscription, and even takes a cut of what it "saves." Recently it moved budgeting — free for years — behind the paywall too.

product.title: Canceling their own subscription — and reaching support — is a battle
product.minus: The bitter irony: canceling Rocket Money itself is as hard as the subscriptions it promised to cancel. Charges continue after cancellation, there's no human to reach — just a chatbot and unanswered emails.

product.title: 2FA and login codes turn into an endless sign-in loop
product.minus: The verification code doesn't arrive, arrives "incorrect," or after a successful login the app boots you right back to the sign-in screen. It's worst for those who changed phone numbers: you can't log in, and can't change the number either.

product.title: Just to see your subscriptions, it demands access to every account and card
product.minus: People come just to see a list of subscriptions and get asked for banks, credit cards, debit cards, even their 401k. For many it's scary enough to uninstall — especially amid complaints that the data is then sold and spam follows.

product.title: The price hides until the end — link everything first, then a $7 charge
product.minus: "Pay what you think is fair" turns into a psychological trap: you pick $0 and are still forced into a $7 minimum. It also grates that the price only shows up after you've already handed over all your data.

product.title: Transactions go missing, duplicate, and count twice — you can't trust the budget
product.minus: Some payments don't pull in, some appear and vanish, income is sometimes counted as spending. You end up double-checking everything by hand, and one false overspend alert nearly gave a user a panic attack.

product.title: Set-and-forget auto-savings genuinely stash money with zero effort
product.plus: Smart auto-savings skim $5–15 at a time toward a goal and won't touch the account if the balance drops below a threshold. For out-of-sight-out-of-mind folks (and ADHD), it quietly builds real sums — one user has $1,025 in each of two pots.

product.title: It surfaces forgotten subscriptions you didn't know about — and that really saves
product.plus: When it works, the headline feature lands: it pulls up long-forgotten and duplicate charges that drained money for months. People name concrete amounts — $100–150 a month on subscriptions they'd forgotten.

product.title: All finances in one place + a bill calendar showing safe-to-spend until payday
product.plus: The most-praised strength is the overview: all accounts, banks and budgets on one screen, clear spending charts, and a calendar of upcoming charges by paycheck. The "safe to spend before next paycheck" view is a standout favorite.

product.title: Category and bill-date guesses often misfire — you fix them by hand
product.minus: The automation misses regularly: no built-in "rent" category, a payment counted as spending, or it shifts recurring-bill dates off the ones you set — risking late fees. Many say the app needs constant babysitting.

product.title: Seeing the real money picture — even a bad one — changes behavior by itself
product.plus: The core emotional value for loyal users isn't a feature but awareness: you finally see where the money goes and stop wasting it. People credit it with breaking the paycheck-to-paycheck cycle, saving for a home, raising their credit score.

product.title: The paywall hits before you've seen the app at all
product.minus: Just to open the app you have to hand over a card for a «7-day trial», and often even that isn't enough: people hit a wall of paywall on the very first screen, before a single useful action. Many read it as a con — let me see what I'm getting into before I open my wallet.

product.title: Bank connections constantly drop
product.minus: The core function — auto-syncing every account — works for many for the first few weeks, then breaks: accounts disconnect every few days, you have to reconnect by hand, and some institutions never link at all. For a paid service it reads as a fatal failure — why pay for the one thing it's supposed to do.

product.title: Plaid spawns duplicates and wipes history
product.minus: The third-party Plaid integration doesn't just break — it duplicates accounts and transactions, and on reconnect deletes old data with no way to merge. People lose months of history; in one case six months vanished and no backup existed.

product.title: Balances show stale — but labelled «just updated»
product.minus: Even when the connection is nominally alive, data refreshes days or weeks late while the app lies that the sync is fresh. For spend-tracking that's lethal — people got caught out trusting Monarch's balance instead of their bank app.

product.title: Forced AI with no real opt-out
product.minus: A recent update jammed AI buttons across the app, at first with no way to disable them, and auto-opted financial data into model training. For a paid finance tool this broke trust the hardest — people refuse to renew over «AI slop» that also gets the numbers wrong.

product.title: Long-promised features moved to a pricey new tier
product.minus: Long-time loyal payers bought into «we pay so the product keeps improving». Then the company split long-requested basic features (retirement planning, separate business expenses) into a new ~$300/yr tier. It feels like bait-and-switch and kills the whole value proposition.

product.title: Best-in-class single-pane view of all finances
product.plus: The big thing people love: everything — accounts, cards, investments, net worth, budgets — gathered in one clean, legible view. For those whose connections work it's a «single pane of glass» that replaced hopping between bank apps, and that alone justifies the subscription.

product.title: The best Mint replacement people have tried
product.plus: After Mint shut down people churned through alternatives and landed on Monarch as the only one that doesn't just match Mint but beats it. Former hardcore Mint users call it «10x what Mint ever was» and move over without regret.

product.title: Powerful rules and customization — but a learning curve
product.plus: Deep customization carries the loyalty: the auto-categorization rule engine, tags, custom categories and budgets let you tailor everything to yourself. The catch is it's not out-of-the-box — it takes hours to learn and can overwhelm an unprepared user.

product.title: Actually changes financial habits and catches junk subscriptions
product.plus: The strongest praise isn't for features but for outcomes: people see for the first time where money leaks, cancel useless subscriptions, and say the app paid for itself in days. Daily reminders to categorize keep them on track and almost make the chore fun.

product.title: A buggy goals update broke what used to work
product.minus: The new goal-tracking beta shipped raw and didn't just fail — it removed a previously loved function, manually tagging transactions to a goal. Goals drift off by thousands, support calls it «unfixable», and users drop their rating specifically over this.

product.title: Sluggish and laggy, especially on Android
product.minus: Even otherwise-happy users find the app noticeably slow: taps take seconds to register, the transaction list reloads and loses your place, and loading on Android hangs with a spinner. For a most-used app that lag turns into a steady irritation.

product.title: Budgeting breaks on mortgages, loans and paychecks
product.minus: For a tool sold on budgeting, the core budget logic limps: mortgage and loan payments don't count as expenses, paychecks aren't registered correctly, and category spend shows as $0. The result: Monarch is good as a retrospective report but not as a live budget.

product.title: Categorization misfires and rewrites what you already reviewed
product.minus: Auto-categorization guesses right about half the time, dumps everything via Google Pay/PayPal into «shopping», and worst of all retroactively rewrites transactions you'd already manually reviewed and marked. Hours of cleanup just to get any meaningful picture.

product.title: Weak, sometimes ghosting support that blames the aggregators
product.minus: When connections break, support doesn't help: tickets sit for weeks, people get called by the wrong name, and blame is shifted to the bank or Plaid instead of being fixed. Worse — a known incompatibility is disclosed only after the subscription auto-renews.

product.title: The price contradicts the very mission of saving
product.minus: $15/mo or ~$99-100/yr strikes many as too steep for an app that promises to help you save — it feels self-contradictory. Some would pay $50/yr and no more; others point out their banks show all accounts for free.

product.title: Bank sync keeps dropping out
product.minus: The core feature — auto-importing transactions — works for the first couple of weeks for many people, then stops syncing: the bank connection drops every few days, you have to keep re-logging in, and support blames the third-party aggregator with no timeline for a fix.

product.title: Breaks right after you pay
product.minus: A recurring story: everything works during the trial, the user buys the annual or lifetime plan — and that same day the sync breaks, and the moment they ask for a refund support goes silent. It's why so many call it a scam.

product.title: Thin bank coverage, especially Canada
product.minus: Bank coverage is narrow: Canadian banks (CIBC, RBC, TD, Wealthsimple, credit unions) and several US ones (Amex, Synchrony, PayPal) are either missing or won't connect via Plaid/Finicity. People bought the plan after seeing their bank listed, only to find it didn't actually work.

product.title: Basics paywalled (2 categories, no manual entry)
product.minus: The free version is artificially crippled to 2-3 budget categories with no manual transaction or income entry, and the limits aren't disclosed up front. People spend an hour setting things up only to hit a "buy premium" wall.

product.title: Surprise charges and you can't cancel
product.minus: Several users report charges they never signed up for, being billed after cancelling the trial, and that cancelling the subscription inside the app simply doesn't work — they get punted to Google.

product.title: Relentless emails you can't unsubscribe from
product.minus: The app floods you with email and push several times a day, and you can't opt out: the unsubscribe link sends you to a login, or support flatly says the only way to stop the automated emails is to delete your account.

product.title: "Free" turns out to be a paywall on the door
product.minus: The site and ads promise a free basic tier, but at sign-up there's only a 7-day trial and a mandatory card — without paying, the app won't let you near your data at all. Many feel tricked.

product.title: "Add transaction" is buried in a menu
product.minus: The single most frequent action — adding an expense — is hidden inside a hamburger menu and takes several taps reaching the top of the screen, where it should be one "+" button. Users call the UI cluttered and unintuitive.

product.title: Auto-categorization and bill detection misfire
product.minus: Auto-categorization is frequently wrong (a mortgage logged under "Shopping" for months), the app invents bills and subscriptions that don't exist while missing real ones, and rules only allow exact matches — so you end up reclassifying everything by hand.

product.title: Credit-card payments and transfers break the math
product.minus: The app double-counts credit-card payments and transfers — cancelling them out or treating an internal transfer as spending; budgets don't roll the leftover into next month, and a changed card number wipes your transaction history.

product.title: When it works, it's a clean Mint replacement
product.plus: For users whose sync holds up, it's loved for being simple and clear: everything on one screen, the In-Pocket feature shows what you can spend without touching savings, auto-rules kill the manual work — and many call it the best replacement for the discontinued Mint.

product.title: One-time lifetime option, not endless subscriptions
product.plus: A lot of people are won over by the option to pay once for lifetime access instead of recurring monthly charges — they call it a decisive advantage over rivals that only offer annual plans.

product.title: Actively developed, with personal support
product.plus: Loyal users note the app is visibly improving: budget rollover and custom rules were added, complaints get fixed, and support sometimes sends a personal email offering help — for some people that outweighs the earlier rough edges.

product.title: The free version hits a hard wall at 10 envelopes
product.minus: Ten envelopes only cover the most primitive budget: people are forced to lump categories together, which defeats the whole point of separate tracking, and the upgrade is a subscription many find absurd.

product.title: Paid means subscription, but people want a one-time buy
product.minus: What puts people off isn't the price so much as the model: a simple envelope tracker charges monthly or yearly, while users would happily pay once — especially those outside the US for whom the subscription is steep.

product.title: Only monthly and yearly — no weekly or biweekly cycles
product.minus: Anyone paid biweekly or weekly can't build a budget around their real cycle: the app only knows monthly and yearly, and for these people that's a straight reason to uninstall.

product.title: Sync failures wipe out data you've already entered
product.minus: An endless "having trouble syncing" spinner, envelopes dropping into the red, and phone-entered transactions vanishing because the server overwrites local records on conflict — fatal for a budget people trust with their money.

product.title: Key actions can only be done on the website
product.minus: Debt, credit-card payments, CSV import, settings edits — the app punts all of these to a browser, and users reasonably ask what the app is even for if it can't do what the web can.

product.title: The envelope method visibly slows your spending
product.plus: Set up envelopes, fill them with money, spend — when one runs out, you stop. A simple, tangible mechanic users credit with real savings: paid-off debt, growing reserves, even a house and a car.

product.title: It never touches your bank — and that's the point
product.plus: Manual entry isn't a bug here, it's the draw: users specifically pick the app because it doesn't demand bank credentials or pull transactions, since hand-logging every spend is exactly what keeps them aware and in control.

product.title: ...yet the missing bank sync is the top wish of the unhappy
product.minus: The same feature becomes a ceiling: with lots of transactions, manual entry is unsustainable, and some people wait years for automatic bank sync, threatening to leave for competitors who have long offered it.

product.title: Ideal for a couple or family on a shared budget
product.plus: Several devices see one budget in real time: spouses log expenses separately but look at the shared picture — it's the most-praised aspect, with some keeping it on their phones for a decade.

product.title: A 90s-looking UI with an on-screen calculator for numbers
product.minus: Text overruns fields and won't scale to the screen, and amounts go in not via the native keyboard but a clunky built-in calculator where you have to poke in the decimal point yourself — even years-long loyalists beg for a fix.

product.title: Income duplicates and envelopes do the math wrong
product.minus: Entered income doubles itself, envelopes don't subtract spending or simply never update the balance — and a budget that can't add up is useless by definition, which stings most for paying users.

product.title: Your draft is wiped the moment you switch apps
product.minus: Open a calculator or your banking app to check a figure and all the unsaved input resets to zero; it quietly enrages people during reconciliation and has gone unfixed for years.

product.title: An un-dismissable location prompt on every transaction
product.minus: On every entry the app demands location access, and even after dozens of refusals and disabling the feature in settings it keeps asking — loyal users dock their rating specifically over this.

product.title: Support is responsive and rescues the rating
product.plus: The team replies fast to emails and comments — many bump their review from 2-3 to 5 stars right after a support exchange; for some that's the deciding plus, though others are annoyed by email-only help with no in-app answers.

product.title: «Free» turns out to be a trial that flips to a subscription
product.minus: People install it believing it's free, spend time entering data and signing up, then hit an $79.99/year or $17–20/month paywall. The irony stings: an app that promises to get you out of debt asks you to add one more bill.

product.title: After an update you simply can't sign in — it hangs on the login screen
product.minus: The single most common technical complaint: an update breaks login. Buttons press but do nothing, the screen hangs grey, the app bounces you to a webpage that never loads. Reinstalling, password resets and cache clears don't help, and years of data become unreachable.

product.title: You have to sort every single transaction by hand
product.minus: By design the app categorizes nothing automatically — you drag every purchase into its line and re-set the budget from scratch each month. For some that manual friction is deliberate «accountability»; for others it's tedious busywork that sends them back to Excel.

product.title: Bank sync lags for days and spawns duplicate transactions
product.minus: Even on premium, transactions import 2–4 days late, you must constantly reconnect the bank, and a single purchase sometimes duplicates two to four times. To know your balance you end up opening your bank app anyway — defeating the whole «real-time budget» promise.

product.title: Every update makes the app worse and more bloated
product.minus: Long-time users say it in one voice: the app used to be great, then updates removed handy features, hid them behind premium, and piled on an intrusive home screen, pop-ups, «lessons» and ads. A budgeting tool is being turned into an everything-app.

product.title: Charges land suddenly and without warning
product.minus: People get billed immediately instead of after the promised 7 days, are charged $79.99 after cancelling, and get no heads-up email before annual renewal. For a debt-strapped audience, a surprise $80 hit feels like a blow from the very people preaching thrift.

product.title: The budget assumes you know your income upfront — irregular pay breaks it
product.minus: The method is built on a projected monthly income, so with unstable or weekly pay the app still shows the full projected amount as available to spend. For variable earners, working out the real balance is nearly impossible — Excel ends up more flexible.

product.title: The math doesn't add up: the remaining balance is wrong
product.minus: Users catch the app in plain arithmetic errors: «remaining to spend» doesn't match what's actually left, a category turns red as overspent when it isn't, and plan/spent/remaining figures simply don't reconcile. For a budgeting app, broken math undermines the one thing it must get right.

product.title: The «every dollar a job» method actually changes habits and clears debt
product.plus: The headline praise: the zero-based approach forces you to name a purpose for every dollar, users finally see where money leaks, find hundreds of dollars of «margin» and genuinely pay down debt. Many say it changed how their household handles money.

product.title: The paycheck planner shows how much money you'll have on any day of the month
product.plus: A favorite among regulars: the paycheck planner spreads income and expenses across dates and shows how much you should have on any given day. It removes the manual «will I make it to next payday» math and makes cash flow predictable.

product.title: Shared budgeting gets spouses onto the same financial page
product.plus: Couples single out the shared access: both partners see the budget, the numbers «don't lie», and for the first time they can agree on spending without fights. For many it's less an accounting tool than a marriage-communication one.

product.title: The free version works for manual tracking, and premium pays for itself via auto-import
product.plus: Despite paywall complaints, a chunk of users are happy: the free tier is enough for manual budgeting if you log in daily, and premium's automatic bank import saves time and, they say, pays for itself in money saved within the first month.

product.title: The paywall greets you before the product does
product.minus: The subscription is demanded on the very first screen: you create an account and the «choose a plan» prompt is already there. You can't even add a second wallet, connect a bank, or look around without paying. Users compare it to paying the restaurant cover charge before seeing the menu.

product.title: The upsell hits even the people who already paid
product.minus: Every launch greets you with a full-screen «limited time» subscription promo — and even Premium and Lifetime users see it. The close (X) icon often doesn't respond to taps. People say outright they're considering switching purely because of this spam.

product.title: After the update the app opens on your very first transaction
product.minus: A fresh bug: on every launch the timeline jumps back to the earliest month (2015/2016/2021), so to log a new transaction you have to scroll through years of data. Many dropped their rating from 5 to 1-2 stars over exactly this: «it was perfect, now it's barely usable».

product.title: Bank connection simply never completes
product.minus: A pervasive bug: after authorizing at the bank (via Plaid or the bank site) the app dumps you back on the Spendee homepage and never applies the connection. People run the flow 3-4 times, hit a white screen or a broken deep-link redirect — and for a paid feature that's an immediate dealbreaker.

product.title: Degrading performance: slower year after year
product.minus: Since the «big update» the app turned sluggish: 7-second cold start, 20-30 seconds to add a transaction, lag even on flagship phones. Long-time users (since 2015) say they'd rather see optimization than «trendy» AI features. Support suggests a reinstall — and nothing else.

product.title: Local banks unsupported — useless outside a handful of countries
product.minus: The headline feature — bank sync — is dead for most markets: India, Mexico, Peru, Colombia, Malaysia, Vietnam, New Zealand, Somalia. Some places offer 3 banks, others just throw «error occurred». And you only find out after signing up and handing over your data.

product.title: The free trial turns into an instant charge
product.minus: The ad promises a 7-day free trial, but the card is charged immediately — with no way to exit the trial. Users demand refunds that aren't granted and call the scheme worthy of a store ban. Some report double charges and an annual fee with no warning.

product.title: Abandonment: years with no new features except «trendy» AI
product.minus: Users since 2014 feel the app is an abandoned project: long-promised small fixes never ship, widgets were removed 5 years ago and never restored, tablet mode was cut. Meanwhile a useless Magic AI Scan and an NFT feature appeared — and the scan even covers up the labels list.

product.title: Real-time cross-platform sync — the reason people stay
product.plus: The standout strength: one account works on Android, iOS, and the browser with data updating in real time across every device. It's web-based, not local storage, so your data isn't trapped on one phone — this is what users put up with everything else for.

product.title: Clean, beautiful, intuitive interface — the thing people love
product.plus: The design is consistently called one of the most beautiful among budget trackers: clean minimalist UI, excellent UX, colorful categories, and clear visualization of spending. For many it's the simplicity and pleasant look that make effortless tracking possible.

product.title: Support that actually fixes things — but often only after a public review
product.plus: When support engages, it often delivers: full refunds, a fixed build within a week, hands-on help with a local New Zealand bank. The catch — many only get a reply after leaving a public review, and some tickets sit unanswered for weeks.

product.title: Multi-currency wallets and budgets — for people living across borders
product.plus: Multi-currency support, shared wallets, and clear charts make Spendee handy for families, couples, and anyone spending across currencies. Custom categories and colored tags let people organize their tracking exactly the way they want.

product.title: Missing basics: split transactions, subcategories, a widget, and CSV import
product.minus: Even happy users list the gaps: you can't split one transaction across categories, there are no subcategories, no home-screen widget for quick entry, and no CSV import from a bank. Some leave for Wallet specifically over split transactions and a cheaper lifetime plan.

product.title: Credit cards and debts break the net-worth math
product.minus: Link a credit card or a loan and its balance adds to your net worth instead of subtracting, while card payments show up as income. There's no way to mark an account as «debt». For anyone who wants to see real free money, the tool simply doesn't work here.

product.title: Paywalled export holds your own data hostage
product.minus: Exporting your full history requires Premium, and even then it caps at 365 days — years of older data stay locked away. Users call it extortion and a GDPR violation; for some the export glitches out entirely. Leaving the app with your own records is hard.

product.title: Bank sync is the defining failure: it breaks after a few days and stays broken for months
product.minus: People buy premium specifically for bank auto-sync, yet it drops after 2-3 days, demands constant reauthorization, and sits unfixed for months — the core paid feature simply stops working.

product.title: You can't create top-level categories — only sub-sub-categories
product.minus: Everyone has a different spending structure, but the app forces its own bloated list and won't let you add a new category — only nest under an existing subcategory, which pushes many users to give up.

product.title: Support is effectively dead — even for premium customers
product.minus: A bot answers everything, users get ghosted after the first reply, acknowledged bugs go unfixed for months, and at times the ticket option was removed entirely — paying customers are left alone with broken features.

product.title: Bought premium, then discovered their bank isn't supported
product.minus: There's no clear warning about bank support before payment: users from India, Mexico, Vietnam, Kazakhstan and elsewhere pay for lifetime premium for sync, only to find their bank simply isn't on the list.

product.title: The best tracker for people who log everything manually
product.plus: Even with no bank sync at all, the app shines in manual mode: easy to enter and categorize spending and see the full picture across accounts — which is exactly why many love it for years.

product.title: Lifetime license instead of endless subscription — users love it
product.plus: The option to pay once for lifetime access instead of subscribing forever is a decisive plus for many and the reason they switched over from competitors like YNAB.

product.title: Records and entire accounts vanish; sync duplicates and deletes data
product.minus: Users lose data: transactions and whole accounts disappear, sync creates duplicates when shared, and deleting an account wipes its entire history — making it impossible to trust as a system of record.

product.title: Sudden logouts and data loss after forced sign-in
product.minus: The app increasingly logs people out on its own and then won't let them back in while their data appears gone; a forced mandatory sign-in on update also wiped the old records of offline users.

product.title: Clean, intuitive interface with clear visual charts
product.plus: A simple, pleasant interface with pie charts and graphs gives an instant view of spending by category — the single most praised thing on the positive side.

product.title: Intrusive premium ads on the home screen
product.minus: Constant pop-up upgrade banners annoy even paying users — to the point of getting notifications to upgrade a lifetime license to a lifetime license.

product.title: Bank sync demands you hand over your online banking login, password and OTP
product.minus: To import transactions the app asks for your net-banking username, password and OTP — which alarms many users who just want offline tracking without surrendering banking access.

product.title: Growing slowness, bugs and freezes, especially after updates
product.minus: Users say every update breaks something: the app lags, hangs, shows blank screens, search stops working — and bugs flagged years ago remain unfixed.

product.title: Billed for subscription even after uninstalling
product.minus: Some users report billing trouble: charged for months after uninstalling, paid premium never activated, and refund requests ignored.

product.title: Reliable cross-device sync of your own data plus web access
product.plus: Setting banks aside, syncing your own records across phone, tablet and the web version is praised as fast and reliable — a key plus for people working across several devices.

product.title: Clean, simple interface is the core reason for love and years of loyalty
product.plus: Users describe it in one word: simple, clean, no useless noise. Many have stayed 7-10 years precisely for the minimalism and clarity — you see where you stand financially without overload.

product.title: Ads pop up at the exact moment of entering an amount — breaking quick logging
product.minus: Ads appear precisely when someone is trying to quickly log a transaction, which makes the app useless in real-world haste. Some complaints are mild (manageable), but many say it's the ad mid-entry that breaks them.

product.title: Bought premium — ads came back after the update
product.minus: Paid premium systematically breaks after each update: ads come back, premium resets, and the only workaround is to uninstall and reinstall the app without updating. People openly call it fraud given that they paid.

product.title: Backup is manual Google Drive only — people lose years of data when changing phones
product.minus: No automatic cloud and no login on a new device: users don't realize backup must be turned on manually, switch phones, and lose all their years of transactions. Even those who set up Google Drive sometimes find auto-backup silently failing, needing manual runs.

product.title: No cross-device sync — couples can't run a budget together
product.minus: The most common request: sync between phone, tablet, and across Android and iPhone. One account doesn't work on multiple devices even with the same email, so couples can't keep shared expenses in one place.

product.title: No automatic SMS bank-parsing — the top wish of manual-entry users
product.minus: Logging is fully manual, and many trust the data because of it, but a huge share wish for automatic transaction reading from bank SMS — it would save tons of time. For those who have SMS parsing, it breaks over phone language or just doesn't fire.

product.title: Double-entry accounts deliver serious tracking of income, expenses and transfers
product.plus: Under the minimalist shell is real bookkeeping: multiple accounts, transfers between them, transparent double-entry. For those who know debit/credit, it reads as a full accounting tool, not just an expense notepad.

product.title: Subcategories exist, but their totals are never summed anywhere
product.minus: You can create subcategories within a category, but the app only shows the parent category's total, not the sum per subcategory. To find out how much went to Transport inside Other, users hit a wall — there's no subtotal and no nesting deeper than one level.

product.title: Multi-currency works for trips, but breaks when changing the main currency
product.minus: For a one-off trip with several currencies it's smooth — set rates, get totals. But the moment you need to change the main currency (moved countries, picked wrong at setup), exchange rates recalculate old transactions so all balances go wrong, and you can't just change the currency without losing data.

product.title: Editing an amount wipes the whole number instead of one digit — a maddening detail
product.minus: You can't delete a single digit when editing an amount — the app wipes the whole number and makes you retype it. There's no copy-paste either. Against otherwise convenient entry, this small thing irritates people the most.

product.title: Strong on spending control, but hides wealth growth: savings and investments look like money is gone
product.minus: For discipline and daily spending control the app is excellent, but money moved into savings or investments is treated as gone — real net-worth growth stays invisible. There's no unified view combining cash, savings and assets into one historical trajectory, and holdings like stocks and crypto must be updated manually.

product.title: Free with no forced subscription — a thing people love on its own
product.plus: The core features are fully usable for free with no pressure to subscribe, and users praise this as a standalone point — some buy premium out of gratitude and for the long haul, not because they're forced to.

product.title: Lifetime license revoked overnight with no warning
product.minus: People who bought a "lifetime" premium years ago suddenly find it gone after an update and are pushed onto a paid subscription — no email, no warning.

product.title: Update logs you out and password reset never arrives
product.minus: After the update users are logged out and can't get back in: the password-reset email never arrives, and there's no sign-up button in the app.

product.title: Years of financial records wiped by the update
product.minus: Users lose 3-6 years of accumulated history: after logging back in the account is empty, and restoring from backup simply doesn't work.

product.title: Support is silent on every request
product.minus: Emails to support go unanswered for weeks: even paid-license holders who attach receipts and GPA numbers get no reply at all.

product.title: New subscription price is several times the old one
product.minus: The subscription arrived priced many times higher than the old one-off purchase — for a budgeting app this feels like a slap in the face.

product.title: Basic everyday features locked behind the paywall
product.minus: Even basic actions became paid: adding a spend to your main wallet, keeping more than one account or category, or exporting your own data.

product.title: Currency conversion broke: everything recalculated 1-to-1
product.minus: After the update multi-currency tracking broke — all past foreign-currency operations were retroactively recalculated at 1:1, making the stats meaningless.

product.title: Cloud sync was first removed, leaving local backup only
product.minus: The main reason people bought premium — syncing across devices — was at one point cut without warning and replaced with local backup only, costing people their data when switching phones.

product.title: Clean, fast interface — the reason people love it
product.plus: Despite the scandal, the app itself is praised for a thoughtful, light, uncluttered interface: logging spends is fast and the spending picture is clear at a glance.

product.title: No bank linking — data stays on your phone
product.plus: Part of the appeal is that it doesn't connect to your bank accounts and keeps your finances local, with nothing sent to someone else's server.

product.title: For the lucky ones, license and data restore via a workaround
product.plus: Some users did get their lifetime access and data back: export a backup, clear Play Store cache, reinstall and sign in with the same Google account — the developer honored the old purchases.

product.title: Top request — attach a receipt photo to a transaction
product.minus: The most common request from happy users is the ability to attach a photo or scan of a receipt to an expense — a feature that's persistently missing.

product.title: The app is nearly impossible to find in the Play Store
product.minus: After returning to the store the app stopped showing up in search — fans complain they can't recommend it to friends and suspect a shadow ban.

product.title: Autofill fires intermittently and misses password fields
product.minus: The most common pain: autofill works one moment and not the next, fails to detect input fields, and forces users to manually copy login and password. For the core reason people install a manager, that defeats the whole point.

product.title: Search removed from the autofill screen — you can't link a login anymore
product.minus: A recent update removed the search button during autofill: when the manager picks the wrong login, you can no longer find and insert the right one manually — you have to leave the app and copy fields by hand. Many openly threaten to switch.

product.title: Keeps demanding the master password and ignores the PIN you set
product.minus: The app repeatedly asks for the master password instead of the PIN or biometrics you configured, even mid-session. You used to be able to sign in without exposing the master password — now you must type it over and over, which is both insecure and maddening.

product.title: Forced accessibility-service consent blocks you out of the app
product.minus: After an update a notice about the “optional” accessibility autofill appears, but the only button is “Accept”: refuse it and you can't open the app at all, locked away from your own passwords.

product.title: Crashes on launch and freezes on a range of Android devices
product.minus: On newer Android handsets (Xiaomi, OnePlus, Samsung) the app crashes right at startup or freezes after login, and neither reinstalling nor clearing the cache helps — access to passwords disappears entirely.

product.title: Nagging review-prompt pop-ups get in the way of actual use
product.minus: The “rate us” dialog pops up exactly when someone is urgently trying to grab a password — even after repeated “not now” taps. It reads as poor UX.

product.title: Forget the master password and you're permanently locked out
product.minus: If the master password suddenly stops being recognized or is forgotten, there's no reset: the site only offers an emailed hint, you can't sign in on a new device, and you can't even delete the account. Several users lost access to all their accounts, including crypto wallets.

product.title: Broken sync strands new passwords — and your work laptop access
product.minus: Saved passwords and authenticator codes sometimes fail to sync across devices, and self-hosters report that updates break Vaultwarden login. One user updated a work password, it didn't sync, and they were locked out of their own laptop.

product.title: Open source with zero-knowledge encryption of your vault
product.plus: The headline reason for the love: the project is open source, transparent, and encrypts everything on-device — passwords, usernames, notes, custom fields — so the service itself has zero knowledge of your vault. For a password manager, that's the very foundation of trust.

product.title: The free tier covers everything an average person needs
product.plus: The free version is powerful, ad-free, and fully featured — many buy a subscription just to support the devs rather than out of need. The paid plan, meanwhile, is described as remarkably cheap.

product.title: Seamless sync across every OS, device and browser
product.plus: When it works, cross-platform is the killer feature: one encrypted vault syncs across macOS, Windows, Linux, Android and iOS and every browser, plus a web vault and portable access. Sharing household logins via organizations and folders is easy.

product.title: Self-hosting via Vaultwarden — a haven for control and privacy
product.plus: Power users love being able to stand up their own Bitwarden or Vaultwarden server and keep passwords entirely under their own control; paired with Tailscale the Android client runs essentially flawlessly. That same community reacts sharply to news about the new CEO and the fate of the free tier.

product.title: A years-trusted password generator that just keeps working
product.plus: The loyalty backbone — people keep every password here for 5–10 years without a single failure, prize the strong generator, and value that it “just works” and stays out of the way. For many it's cheaper than their old LastPass or Roboform with no loss of features.

product.title: Android autofill is the core pain: it doesn't trigger, forcing manual copy-paste
product.minus: Dozens of users report the app stops detecting login and password fields — especially in Chrome, Brave and Firefox — so instead of the promised autofill they have to open 1Password itself and copy the password by hand. Many note it used to work and has degraded over the past year.
